Multiple-Factor Confirmatory Factor Analysis Model

Source: R/fa_confirmatory.R
fa_confirmatory.Rd

Fits a confirmatory factor analysis model with one or more factors, where each factor is specified by naming its indicator variables and the measurement structure is specified by describing what is constrained (equal_loading, equal_intercept, equal_error) rather than by more technical terms. The function then reports which classical measurement structure the description implies (congeneric, essentially tau-equivalent, tau-equivalent, essentially parallel, or parallel), the parameter estimates with confidence intervals, fit information, and, per factor, coefficient omega, the average variance extracted (AVE), and coefficient H, each with a delta method standard error and confidence interval computed by lavaan from defined parameters (no additional packages are involved). cfa_k() is an alias of this function.

Usage

fa_confirmatory(
  data = NULL,
  factors,
  S = NULL,
  N = NULL,
  M = NULL,
  equal_loading = FALSE,
  equal_intercept = FALSE,
  equal_error = FALSE,
  correlated_factors = TRUE,
  meanstructure = NULL,
  estimator = "ML",
  missing = "fiml",
  ordered = NULL,
  se = NULL,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  output = c("verbose", "measurement", "summary", "standardized", "fit"),
  ...,
  wald_df = Inf,
  rmsea_conf_level = 0.9
)

cfa_k(
  data = NULL,
  factors,
  S = NULL,
  N = NULL,
  M = NULL,
  equal_loading = FALSE,
  equal_intercept = FALSE,
  equal_error = FALSE,
  correlated_factors = TRUE,
  meanstructure = NULL,
  estimator = "ML",
  missing = "fiml",
  ordered = NULL,
  se = NULL,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  output = c("verbose", "measurement", "summary", "standardized", "fit"),
  ...,
  wald_df = Inf,
  rmsea_conf_level = 0.9
)

Arguments

data

A raw data matrix or data frame, rows are respondents and columns include the items named in factors. Supply exactly one of data or S.

factors

Named list. Each element names a factor and gives the character vector of its indicator columns (two or more per factor; three or more when only one factor is specified). Each item loads on exactly one factor (simple structure). An item that is not a column of data or an item of S is refused with an error of class dmar_items_invalid (see dmar_metadata).

S

A symmetric covariance matrix of the items, with dimnames naming the items; N is then required. Supply exactly one of data or S.

N

Total sample size. Required with S; ignored (inferred from the rows) with data.

M

Optional named numeric vector of item means, used with a covariance matrix to model the mean structure (required there when equal_intercept is used). Ignored for raw data.

equal_loading

Logical, or a named logical vector with one element per factor. TRUE constrains the loadings within a factor to a single value (across factors nothing is equated). Defaults to FALSE.

equal_intercept

Logical, or a named logical vector with one element per factor. TRUE constrains the item intercepts within a factor to a single value; this requires the mean structure (raw data, or M with a covariance matrix). Defaults to FALSE.

equal_error

Logical, or a named logical vector with one element per factor. TRUE constrains the error variances within a factor to a single value. Defaults to FALSE.

correlated_factors

Logical. If TRUE (default) the factors covary freely; because each factor variance is fixed to 1, the phi terms for factor pairs are the latent correlations. If FALSE the factor covariances are fixed to zero.

meanstructure

Logical or NULL. NULL (default) models the mean structure exactly when it is needed: under FIML or two-stage estimation of raw data (the default, so the item intercepts, the nu rows, join the table), when any equal_intercept is TRUE, or when M is supplied. Set TRUE to model intercepts regardless (raw data or M required), or FALSE to suppress them (an error if equal_intercept is used).

estimator

Character; estimator passed to lavaan. Must be one of "ML" (default; maximum likelihood, fully efficient under multivariate normality), "MLR" (robust maximum likelihood, raw data required: maximum likelihood estimates with the test statistic corrected for nonnormality, the scaled statistic of Satorra and Bentler, 1994, in the form Yuan and Bentler, 2000, gave it for incomplete data; its matching Huber-White sandwich standard errors are used when se is omitted), "WLS" (the asymptotic distribution free estimator of Browne, 1984; raw data and a large sample required), "WLSMV" (diagonally weighted least squares with mean- and variance-adjusted test statistic; Muthén, 1984; Muthén, du Toit, & Spisic, 1997; the standard choice for ordered categorical items, and what ordered switches to), or "GLS" (generalized least squares; Browne, 1974). With a robust estimator the reported fit indices are the robust versions.

missing

Character; missing-data handling when raw data are supplied: "fiml" (default; full information maximum likelihood, which uses every case with an observed item; lavaan's name "ml" is accepted), "listwise" (listwise deletion), "pairwise" (passed to lavaan, for ordered items), "two_stage" (two-stage maximum likelihood with normal theory standard errors and test), or "robust_two_stage" (two-stage maximum likelihood with standard errors and test robust to nonnormality); lavaan's spellings "two.stage" and "robust.two.stage" are accepted for the last two. See Details for two-stage estimation. Ignored with S, except that a two-stage request with S is an error, since a covariance matrix has no incomplete cases. With ordered items, "ml"/"fiml" and the two-stage options are not available; use "pairwise" or "listwise". FIML needs a maximum likelihood estimator of continuous items with normal theory or Huber-White standard errors. When the default meets ordered items, a least squares estimator ("WLS", "WLSMV", "GLS"), se = "robust.sem", or a Satorra-Bentler kind of test passed through ..., the items are fitted as they stand if no item value is missing (listwise deletion then deletes nothing), and otherwise the call stops and names the option to choose, rather than deleting cases unasked. With complete data FIML and listwise deletion give the same estimates and the same chi square, and for estimator = "ML" the same fit indices; the standard errors differ slightly, since FIML takes them from the observed information, as lavaan does and as Savalei (2010) recommends with incomplete data, and listwise deletion from the expected information.

ordered

Ordered categorical items: NULL (none, the default), TRUE (every item), or a character vector of item names. Requires raw data. Each factor must be all ordered or all continuous. Declaring ordered items switches the estimator to "WLSMV" (with a message, unless a categorical estimator was requested), fits thresholds in place of intercepts, and reports each ordered factor's omega on the categorical sum score metric (categorical omega with the unrestricted polychoric denominator); see Details.

se

Standard error method passed to lavaan. The default, NULL, follows the estimator: model-based "standard" errors for ML, GLS and WLS; Huber-White sandwich "robust.huber.white" errors for MLR; and "robust.sem" errors for WLSMV. Explicit compatible choices are retained. The ML and MLR point estimates use the same likelihood; their standard errors and tests use different reference assumptions. This difference does not depend on whether optimization is iterative or an equivalent solution is computed analytically. "robust.sem" requires complete data and is refused with FIML; use "robust.huber.white" to retain incomplete respondents. No standard-error request silently changes the missing-data treatment. "none" requests point estimates only. Under two-stage estimation the matching corrected two-stage errors are used; se must be NULL, "standard", or "none". MLR and Huber-White errors require raw data. Robust SEM errors from covariance input require ML and a matching NACOV in ....

conf_level

Confidence level for the parameter confidence intervals, including the delta method intervals for omega, AVE, and H. Defaults to 0.95. It does not reach the RMSEA interval, whose level is rmsea_conf_level.

output

Format of the returned object:

"verbose"

(default) Parameter estimates with confidence intervals, the per-factor defined parameters (loading_sum, error_sum, omega, ave, H), and fit information.

"measurement"

The measurement-property rows only: per factor omega, ave, and H (with delta method standard errors and confidence intervals), the latent correlation phi for every factor pair (with its confidence interval), and, for raw data, the heterotrait-monotrait ratio htmt for every factor pair via htmt.

"summary"

The raw summary() output from lavaan (not a data frame).

"standardized"

The standardized parameter estimates from lavaan::standardizedSolution(), whose defined rows describe the standardized items: omega there is the reliability of the unit-weighted sum of the standardized items, while ave and H do not depend on the metric of the items and equal the rows of the other tables. For a factor with equal_loading or equal_error these rows are computed from each item's own standardized loading and error variance (see The standardized solution under Details of fa_confirmatory). Under se = "none" the se, z, pvalue, ci.lower, and ci.upper columns are NA.

"fit"

The raw lavaan fit object. Escape hatch for direct lavaan access, including likelihood ratio tests between two fa_confirmatory() fits via lavaan::lavTestLRT().

...

Additional arguments forwarded to lavaan (e.g., cluster or bootstrap). A group argument is an error: see Details for why, and measurement_invariance for the model in several groups.

wald_df

The reference distribution of the Wald intervals and p-values of the parameter rows: Inf (the default), the normal distribution, which leaves lavaan's intervals and p-values as they are; a single positive number, the degrees of freedom of a t distribution for every parameter row, the intervals and p-values recomputed from the same estimates and standard errors; or "missing_information", von Hippel's (2016) degrees of freedom \(\max\{3, N(1 - \gamma_j) - 1\}\) for each loading, from its fraction of missing information \(\gamma_j\) (\(N - 1\) with complete data), with every other row left on the normal reference. A number applies to the tables of output = "verbose", "measurement", and "standardized", the keyword to that of "verbose" only (the "measurement" table has no loading), and either needs standard errors other than "none" and "bootstrap"; the keyword also needs the fits its calibration covers, maximum likelihood (estimator = "ML" or "MLR") of continuous items by FIML or with complete data, with normal theory or Huber-White standard errors. Anything else is an error that says why. It follows ..., so it must be named in full. See Details.

rmsea_conf_level

Confidence level of the RMSEA interval of the fit rows, which the rmsea_ci_level row records. Defaults to 0.90, the conventional level, whose limits decide the tests of close and not close fit at .05 (see sem_fit_measures); rmsea_conf_level = 0.95 gives a 95 percent interval. It sets the level in the table DMAR returns and in its glance(); output = "summary" returns the lavaan summary, which shows lavaan's 90 percent interval whatever this argument is.

Value

For output = "verbose" (default) and output = "measurement", a data.frame (classes dmar_fa_confirmatory, dmar_cfa_k, and dmar_tbl) with columns syntax, term, estimate, se, test_statistic, p_value, ci_lower, ci_upper. The "model" attribute is a named character vector giving, per factor, the implied classical structure; the printed header displays it. For output = "verbose" the "test" attribute names the statistic in the chi_square row: "standard", "scaled" (a robust or categorical estimator), or, under the two-stage options, the two-stage residual based or scaled statistic; a two-stage fit also carries the "two_stage" attribute, a list with the method, the lines printed under the table, and, in rows, the cases the first stage read and lavaan's count of them when an auxiliary variable was named, and the "fit_rows" attribute holds the lines that name the version of the indices after FIML estimation and the SRMR of a model with a mean structure (NULL when there are none). The tables of "verbose" and "measurement" also carry the "wald_df" attribute, the degrees of freedom of the t reference of their intervals and p-values (Inf for the normal one); under wald_df = "missing_information" it holds the degrees of freedom of each loading in the table, named by term (the other rows keep the normal reference), the "wald_df_table" attribute is the df_missing table they came from, and "wald_df_rows" names what they are. For output = "summary", the lavaan summary object; for "standardized", the standardized solution, with the same "wald_df" attribute; for "fit", the lavaan fit object.

Details

With ordered items, the model is fit by WLSMV to polychoric correlations with thresholds. A sum score of ordered items lives on the metric of the observed categories, not on the latent response metric of the polychoric loadings, so for a factor whose items are ordered the reported omega is categorical omega, the reliability of the sum of the observed categories (Green & Yang, 2009), computed from the same fit with the total variance built from the unrestricted polychoric correlations (Kelley & Pornprasertmanit, 2016, Eq. 18), the default denominator of reliability_omega_categorical; the substitution is announced in a message and recorded in the omega_metric attribute, and the delta method interval columns are NA for those rows because the delta method interval describes the latent response metric. When the data do not determine a polychoric correlation among a factor's items (a bivariate table with empty cells, as two items skewed in opposite directions produce), that factor's omega is NA with a warning naming the pair. AVE and coefficient H concern the latent response correlations themselves and are reported unchanged on that metric. An improper solution (a negative error variance) leaves some of these properties undefined, and their rows are then NA with a warning; see Details. For a bootstrap confidence interval on a categorical omega, use reliability_omega_categorical on the factor's items.

cfa_1 and cfa_2 are convenience wrappers around this function for the one and two factor cases: cfa_1() takes a vector of items and fits one factor over them, and cfa_2() takes the items of each of two factors. Both forward every argument here, so their results are this function's results, with the factors named f1 (and f2).

Describing the model instead of naming it. The classical measurement structures are nested patterns of within-factor equality constraints (Lord & Novick, 1968; Graham, 2006):

congeneric

loadings, intercepts, and error variances all free.

essentially tau-equivalent

equal loadings; intercepts and error variances free.

tau-equivalent

equal loadings and equal intercepts; error variances free.

essentially parallel

equal loadings and equal error variances; intercepts free.

parallel

equal loadings, equal intercepts, and equal error variances.

The caller states the constraints; the function reports the implied name, per factor, in the printed header and in the "model" attribute of the returned table. The distinction between tau-equivalent and essentially tau-equivalent (and between parallel and essentially parallel) lives entirely in the mean structure: the covariance structure of the two members of each pair is identical, so without intercepts in the model only the "essentially" form can be claimed. That is why equal_intercept requires raw data or M: covariances alone cannot speak to it. A constraint pattern outside the classical list (for example equal error variances with free loadings) is fit as requested and labeled descriptively, since it has no conventional name.

Identification fixes each factor variance to 1 (and each factor mean to 0 when the mean structure is modeled), so all loadings are estimated and within-factor equality constraints are meaningful. Two fa_confirmatory() fits that differ only in descriptor settings are nested, so output = "fit" feeds lavaan::lavTestLRT() directly (with estimator = "MLR", lavaan applies the scaled difference test).

Measurement properties. For factor \(f\) with unstandardized loadings \(\lambda_j\) and error variances \(\psi_j\) (factor variance 1): coefficient omega \(= (\sum_j \lambda_j)^2 / ((\sum_j \lambda_j)^2 + \sum_j \psi_j)\) (McDonald, 1999), the reliability of the unit-weighted composite; the average variance extracted \(= J^{-1} \sum_j \lambda_j^2 / (\lambda_j^2 + \psi_j)\) (Fornell & Larcker, 1981), the mean proportion of item variance the factor accounts for; and coefficient \(H = (1 + (\sum_j \lambda_j^2/\psi_j)^{-1})^{-1}\) (Hancock & Mueller, 2001), the reliability of the optimally weighted composite, which no single item can drag below its value for any subset. All three are computed as lavaan defined parameters, so each carries a delta method standard error and a conf_level confidence interval in the same table as the model parameters. The limits of all three are formed on the logit scale from that standard error and transformed back to the scale of the coefficient (Browne, 1982; the confidence interval transformation principle of Kelley, 2007: the limits of a monotone transformation of a parameter are the transformation of its limits), as reliability_H and fa_exploratory form those of H by default, so they lie within (0, 1) and are asymmetric near one, as the sampling distribution of a high reliability is; for H with one factor they are the limits those two functions give the same fit. The se column is the standard error of the coefficient itself. lavaan's own limits for these defined parameters, the estimate plus or minus the normal quantile times the standard error, can exceed one.

The standardized solution. With output = "standardized" the defined rows are evaluated at the standardized values: the standardized loading \(s_j = \lambda_j / (\lambda_j^2 + \psi_j)^{1/2}\) and error variance \(e_j = \psi_j / (\lambda_j^2 + \psi_j)\) of each item take the places of \(\lambda_j\) and \(\psi_j\) in the formulas above (for an ordered item, those of its latent response). Omega is then the reliability of the unit-weighted sum of the standardized items, which differs from the omega of the sum of the items as they are scored whenever the items' variances differ; the average variance extracted and H are the same on either scale. lavaan evaluates a defined parameter at the standardized values of the labels it names, and a label that equal_loading or equal_error gives several items has one unstandardized value but a standardized value for each item, which differ when the items' variances differ; lavaan uses the first item's. For such a factor the rows are computed here from every item's own \(s_j\) and \(e_j\), with delta method standard errors from their derivatives with respect to the free parameters and lavaan's covariance matrix of the estimates (under se = "bootstrap", from lavaan's bootstrap draws), and with the test statistic and p-value, as lavaan forms them for every other row. fa_bifactor does the same for its indices.

Improper solutions. When the error variance \(\psi_j\) of an item is estimated below zero (a Heywood case; for an ordered item, the residual variance of its latent response, which the theta parameterization estimates), the item's communality \(\lambda_j^2 / (\lambda_j^2 + \psi_j)\) exceeds one. The average variance extracted averages the communalities, and coefficient H, the largest reliability that a weighted sum of the items attains, is at least that communality, since the item weighted alone attains it; for such a factor neither is a proportion of variance, so its ave and H rows are NA, with a warning naming the items and their communalities. Omega, the reliability of the unit-weighted sum, depends on the error variances only through their sum, and while that sum is positive it remains a proportion and is reported, as reliability_omega reports it, beside the warning; when the sum is negative the model implies a negative error variance for the sum score and an omega above one, and the omega row is NA as well. Categorical omega is not defined for an improper ordered solution, so an ordered factor's omega row is NA whenever one of its items is improper. On holzinger_swineford, a factor measured by visual perception and lozenges alone, beside one measured by general information, paragraph comprehension, and sentence completion, gives visual perception an error variance below zero and the first factor an H of 1.32; that row is NA, while its omega, .71, is reported. A negative error variance can also mean that the likelihood has no maximum, the variance falling without bound while the likelihood still rises and lavaan's optimizer stopping where its steps stop gaining; the function checks for this by fitting the model again with the variance held further out (see fa_bifactor) and, when the log likelihood there is higher or lower by no more than \(10^{-6}\) per case, stops for every output with an error of class dmar_no_maximum that prints the lavaan code of the fit, where bounds = "pos.var" (also accepted through ... here) or a different model are the choices. The lavaan fit (output = "fit") keeps the defined parameters as lavaan computes them.

Discriminant validity. Three complementary readings come from output = "measurement": (a) the latent correlation phi for a factor pair, with a confidence interval whose upper limit near 1 means the data cannot distinguish the two factors; (b) the Fornell and Larcker (1981) comparison, which asks whether each factor's ave exceeds the squared phi of its pairs (the factor should share more variance with its own items than with the other factor); and (c) for raw data, the model-free htmt ratio (Henseler, Ringle, & Sarstedt, 2015). A pair whose ratio the data leave undefined, as when some items of two factors are never observed together in a planned missing data design whose forms share other items, has an htmt row of NA, with a warning that names it, while the model based rows are reported: FIML (or two-stage estimation) estimates the latent correlation from the pairs of their items that are observed together, through the factor structure. When no item of one factor is ever observed with an item of the other, as when the two factors were given to different respondents, the latent correlation enters the likelihood only through covariances the data never observe, so it is not identified (the likelihood is flat in it, and lavaan leaves it at its starting value with no standard error, or under two-stage estimation fits it to an arbitrary covariance), and fa_confirmatory() refuses the fit, naming the pair: fit each factor alone, whose omega, ave, and H are identified, or link the forms with items given on both (missing_coverage reports the cases behind every pair of items). Orthogonal factors (correlated_factors = FALSE) are not refused: their correlation is fixed at 0 rather than estimated, so nothing is left unidentified, and since the likelihood then separates into the parts of the factors' items, each factor's omega, ave, and H, with their standard errors, are those of its own one factor fit (to the accuracy of the optimizer). The fit rows of such a fit are lavaan's, whose degrees of freedom count the covariances no case observes among the moments tested (lavaan warns that their coverage is zero), though the data cannot test them; each factor's fit is better judged from its own fit. More generally, when lavaan cannot compute the standard errors of a fit (its information matrix cannot be inverted, which suggests a parameter that is not identified at the estimates), every standard error, test, and interval is NA, with a warning of class dmar_result_qualified, rather than the 0 lavaan reports for the defined quantities. So they are when lavaan computes them from an information matrix that is singular in the directions the equality constraints leave free (scaled to a unit diagonal, its smallest eigenvalue is below \(10^{-6}\)), which it inverts, sometimes with a warning that the covariance matrix of the estimates does not appear to be positive definite and sometimes with none, reporting finite values that do not estimate the sampling variability of the estimates: the observed information of a FIML fit and the expected information of a listwise fit or of a covariance matrix alike, as in fa_bifactor, fa_second_order, and reliability_H. The rows report the numbers and their uncertainty; the judgment is the researcher's.

Two-stage estimation with incomplete data. With missing = "two_stage" the model is estimated in two stages (Yuan & Bentler, 2000; Savalei & Bentler, 2009). The first stage estimates the means and covariances of the items by maximum likelihood under the saturated normal model (the EM estimates), from every case with an observed item and from any auxiliary variables named through lavaan's aux argument, which enter this stage only, so the model itself is untouched by them. A case observed on an auxiliary variable but on no item is used as well: the first stage estimates the items and the auxiliaries jointly, so its auxiliary values inform the item moments, and its likelihood is summed over every case (Savalei & Bentler, 2009, Eq. 10). That is what makes the estimates consistent when the items go missing together at random given the auxiliary variables, the case an auxiliary is named for. lavaan's two-stage estimator reads such a case in its first stage but leaves it out of its sample size, and that sample size turns the per case quantities of the two stages into every standard error (each too large by the square root of the ratio of the two counts), the test statistics, the fit indices, and the information criteria. The fit is therefore computed again with its sample size set to the cases the first stage read, from the same estimates (in one group they do not depend on the sample size), so that every number in the table, and in the lavaan fit of output = "fit", counts them: lavaan's summary() of that fit counts them as used, and lavTestLRT warns that a difference test between it and a fit lavaan made of the same data on its own sample size is invalid. A message says how many such cases there are, and a line under the table names the sample size. When the fit cannot be computed again, a warning says what rests on lavaan's sample size instead. On six Holzinger and Swineford tests with the whole block missing for 77 of 301 pupils, at random given general information (the auxiliary), the standard error of a verbal loading of 2.840 is .190 rather than lavaan's .220. Cases observed only on auxiliary variables are kept, as under FIML. Such cases still contribute to the observed-data likelihood through their auxiliary measurements. The second stage fits the model to those moments with the complete data maximum likelihood discrepancy function. The estimates are consistent when the data are missing at random, as FIML's are, and Savalei and Bentler (2009) found them only marginally less efficient. What the second stage cannot supply alone is a standard error or a test, because it treats the EM moments as the moments of complete data, which makes its naive chi square and standard errors too optimistic. The standard errors are therefore the two-stage sandwich of Savalei and Bentler (2009, Eq. 6), built from the observed information of the saturated model under missing data, and the chi_square row is their residual based statistic (Eq. 8; Eq. 14 with auxiliary variables), which is referred to chi square on the model's degrees of freedom. In their simulations with normal data and 15 or 30 percent of the values missing it rejected a correct model in no more than 9 percent of the tests at the .05 level with samples of 200, where the FIML chi square reached 21.9 percent. With missing = "robust_two_stage" the standard errors are the sandwich that is robust to nonnormality (Yuan & Bentler, 2000) and the chi_square row is lavaan's scaled statistic, the pairing Savalei and Falk (2014) found to outperform robust FIML with incomplete nonnormal data. Under both, cfi and rmsea are lavaan's robust indices, which correct the complete data indices of the second stage for the missing data as Zhang and Savalei (2023) propose: each subtracts from the naive statistic T an estimate c of its expectation under the model, built from the asymptotic covariance matrix of the stage one moments. With missing = "robust_two_stage" that matrix is the sandwich of the observed and first order information of the saturated model, and the indices are their TS V2 (Table 2), the version they recommend after two-stage estimation, for incomplete nonnormal data as well. With missing = "two_stage" it is the inverse of the observed information, the form the sandwich takes under normality, so the indices are the normal theory analog of TS V2, which Zhang and Savalei did not study: it estimates the same population values and agrees closely with TS V2 when the data are normal, but it departs from TS V2 as the data depart from normality, where "robust_two_stage" gives TS V2 itself. On nine Holzinger and Swineford tests with 90 scores on each of two deleted at random, the two RMSEAs are .0869 and .0859. Zhang and Savalei define only the RMSEA and the CFI; the tli and nnfi rows apply the same correction to the Tucker-Lewis index, and the RMSEA interval inverts the scaled statistic T/c and rescales its limits by c, both of them lavaan's extensions. Indices from a FIML fit are never paired with two-stage estimates. The AIC and BIC rows are the two-stage information criteria of Lai (2021), built, like H0 and H1, from the complete data normal log likelihood evaluated at the EM estimates; Lai shows that, unlike the FIML criteria, they select in large samples the model that complete data would select, and they are comparable only with other two-stage fits of the same variables (sem_information_criteria reports the same values). The difference \(-2(H0 - H1)\) is the naive statistic, which is not chi square distributed. Two nested two-stage fits from output = "fit" are compared with lavaan::lavTestLRT(), which applies the scaled difference test (Satorra & Bentler, 2001). The test attribute names the statistic in the chi_square row, and the lines under the printed table say which statistic and indices it reports. Two-stage estimation is a normal theory method for raw continuous data: ordered items, covariance input, and an estimator other than "ML" are refused, robustness coming from "robust_two_stage" rather than from estimator = "MLR". Under "two_stage" the residual based statistic is refused, with a message that points to robust two-stage estimation, for a fit with sampling weights or clustered cases, inequality constraints, or a parameter on a bound passed through ..., since the statistic assumes independent, equally weighted cases and a projection on the parameters left free. The residual based statistic already sums the information of the saturated model over every case the first stage read, so the correction for cases observed on an auxiliary variable alone leaves it as it was.

One group. The model is fit in one group. Every loading, error variance, intercept, and factor correlation carries a label, which is how the equality descriptors and the defined parameters refer to it, and lavaan holds a label shared by several groups equal across them. With group passed through ... the groups would therefore share every measurement parameter, with each factor's variance fixed at 1 (and its mean at 0) in every group: a model of complete invariance rather than a model fit by group, whose omega, ave, and H belong to the pooled model rather than to any one group. A group argument is therefore an error. measurement_invariance fits the model in several groups, beginning with the configural model, which leaves every parameter free in each group; reliability_H reads H for one factor in one group from its fit, and reliability_omega on one group's rows gives that group's omega.

Confidence interval conventions. Parameter rows (including omega, ave, H, and phi) use conf_level, 0.95 by default. The RMSEA interval uses rmsea_conf_level, 0.90 by default, the conventional level for the RMSEA, because a \(100(1 - 2\alpha)\) percent interval decides the one-sided tests of close and not close fit at level \(\alpha\) (MacCallum, Browne, & Sugawara, 1996, p. 136); the rmsea_ci_level row records that level, and the line beneath the printed table names it when it differs from conf_level.

The parameter intervals are Wald intervals, the estimate plus or minus a normal quantile times its standard error, and the p-values refer the ratio of the two (test_statistic) to the normal distribution. The normal reference treats the standard error as known, which it is only in the limit, and in small samples, more so with missing values, the intervals are too short (von Hippel, 2016). wald_df refers both to the t distribution on that many degrees of freedom instead (von Hippel's Eq. 29): the limits become the estimate plus or minus the t quantile times the same standard error (for the omega, AVE, and H rows, on the logit scale) and the p-value is \(2 P(T_\nu > |z|)\); the test_statistic column holds the same ratio under either reference, and a line under the printed table names the reference distribution. One number applies to every parameter row, a sensitivity check of the analyst's own choosing. The fit rows, the RMSEA interval, categorical omega, and the HTMT rows are untouched.

Degrees of freedom from the missing information. With wald_df = "missing_information" each loading gets its own degrees of freedom by von Hippel's (2016, Eqs. 31 and 34) effective sample size rule with \(k = 1\), $$\nu_j = \max\{3, N(1 - \gamma_j) - 1\},$$ where \(N\) is the number of cases the fit used and \(\gamma_j\) the parameter's fraction of missing information, estimated from the fit as fraction_missing_information estimates it (the unstructured estimator of Chen and Savalei, 2021, which cannot be negative); df_missing describes the rule and its floor. A loading of an item that is rarely missing keeps nearly \(N - 1\) degrees of freedom, and with complete data (listwise deletion, or a covariance matrix) every \(\gamma_j\) is 0 and every \(\nu_j\) is \(N - 1\). The "wald_df" attribute holds each parameter's degrees of freedom, the "wald_df_table" attribute the df_missing table they came from, and the line under the printed table names the rule and the rows it applied to.

The rule, and \(k = 1\) rather than \(k\) equal to the number of items or von Hippel's complete data rule (his Eq. 32) on \(N - 1\) or \(N\) less the number of items, come from a calibration study of these intervals under full information maximum likelihood (in the package's source repository, methodology/missing_data). It simulated one factor models as this function writes them (loadings from .8 to .5, the factor variance fixed at 1), with six items at N = 30, 50, 100, and 200 and with 12 items at N = 50 and 100, normal data fit by ML with normal theory standard errors and nonnormal data (the factor and the errors drawn from a standardized chi square on 4 degrees of freedom, skewness 1.41 and excess kurtosis 3) fit by MLR with Huber-White standard errors, with no missing values or with 15 or 30 percent of the values of half the items missing completely at random or at random, in 2000 replications of each of 60 cells; a repetition of von Hippel's own design reproduced the coverage he published to within .012. Under a decision rule fixed before the run (mean absolute distance of the coverage from .95, over the cells with \(N \le 100\) and missing values, below the normal interval's; coverage above .96 in no cell; a mean distance within .005 of the best rule's; the simplest passing rule chosen, a cell's coverage being the mean over the target's parameters), \(k = 1\) passed for the loadings, with a mean distance of .0171 against .0247 for the normal reference and no cell's coverage, averaged over its loadings, above .9502 (single loadings, the largest of 384 with missing values, reached .9595, with a Monte Carlo standard error of .0044, and none exceeded .96), and for omega, .0180 against .0242 with no coverage above .9550. It passed again within the normal theory cells and within the robust ones taken alone. With nonnormal data the intervals still covered below .95 (between .908 and .937 for the loadings, averaged over a cell's loadings), since the robust standard errors themselves are too small at these sample sizes: the t reference narrows the shortfall and does not remove it.

These coverage figures rest on the data sets that the study's eligibility rule for the unrestricted (H1) estimates admitted. The affine-collapse diagnostic sets aside some of those data sets, and the coverage over the data sets that remain has not been established. Replaying the eligibility rule on the raw data cannot by itself validate the refits of the fraction of missing information and the information diagnostics. The keyword is an approximate, opt-in rule, not a coverage guarantee.

The keyword is restricted to the study's estimator and parameter types. The other parameter rows keep the normal reference: the study evaluated the unstandardized loadings and omega, not factor variances or correlations, intercepts, error variances, or the sums, AVE, and H built from them, and nothing shows that the rule suits them; omega passed with its limits formed on its own scale, but its limits here are formed on the logit scale, where the study found the t reference overcovered (.9645 with normal data), so it keeps the normal reference as reliability_omega's logistic intervals do. It is an error with the "measurement" table, which has no loading, with the standardized solution, with an estimator other than ML and MLR or ordered items, with pairwise deletion or two-stage estimation (for which no fraction of missing information is computed), and with standard errors other than the normal theory and Huber-White ones (se = "standard" and "robust.huber.white"; "robust.sem" only under listwise deletion, or from a covariance matrix with the asymptotic covariance matrix of its moments passed to lavaan as NACOV through ..., without which lavaan refuses it, since lavaan computes that sandwich from raw data or a supplied NACOV, and under FIML falls back to listwise deletion, so that missing = "fiml" would not be honored). More generally, it is an error wherever lavaan replaces the FIML fit that missing = "fiml" asks for with a fit to the complete cases, which it also does for a test statistic of the Satorra-Bentler kind passed through ... (test = "satorra.bentler", "mean.var.adjusted", "scaled.shifted", and their corrected forms), whether or not a value is missing: estimator = "MLR", whose scaled statistic is computed under FIML, or the test with missing = "listwise" is the alternative. It is an error, too, where fraction_missing_information cannot compute the fraction for the data: a pair of items that no case observes together, or an unrestricted estimate of the means and covariances that does not exist (see its Fits that are refused). Under FIML the standard errors must come from the observed information computed from the Hessian of the fitted model, lavaan's default there and the one the study used; the first order information and the observed information of the unrestricted model (observed.information = "h1"), which reach lavaan only through ..., are an error. Under listwise deletion (or from a covariance matrix) lavaan's normal theory standard errors use the expected information where the study's cells without missing values used the observed; at N = 30 and 50 they are 1 to 2 percent shorter for the loadings and less than 1 percent shorter for omega, so the complete data intervals here are, if anything, slightly shorter than those the study evaluated, whose coverage with normal data, averaged over a cell's loadings, rose from between .936 and .946 to between .945 and .949 on \(N - 1\) degrees of freedom (single loadings between .934 and .963, where the normal reference reached .962). Several factors, equal loadings, and auxiliary variables are accepted, and the rule is applied to each loading as it stands, which the one factor models of the study support by analogy rather than directly.

Which version of each fit row. With complete continuous data and estimator = "ML" the fit rows are the standard ones, under FIML (the default) as under listwise deletion: with no value missing the FIML corrected indices described below equal them, and no line under the table names a version. With a robust or categorical estimator, chi_square is the scaled statistic and cfi, tli, nnfi, rmsea, and the RMSEA interval are lavaan's robust versions, the corrections sem_fit_measures describes. One version holds all of those rows. For the older mean and variance adjusted statistic (test = "mean.var.adjusted" passed through ...), lavaan computes no robust versions, and they are computed here as sem_fit_measures computes them: Savalei (2018) shows that the robust RMSEA and CFI do not depend on which corrected statistic accompanies them, so they equal those of the Satorra-Bentler statistic of the same fit. Where lavaan did not compute the robust indices of a maximum likelihood fit of continuous items with complete data, the rows hold the standard indices, which estimate the population values of the ML indices with the small sample bias corrected as if the data were normal, and not the scaled ones, which put the scaled statistic into the standard formulas and estimate population values that change with the kurtosis of the data (Savalei, 2018); after FIML or two-stage estimation, and for ordered items or a least squares estimator, they hold its scaled indices, or else its standard ones. A model with no degrees of freedom (one factor of three items, say) fits exactly in every version: its cfi is 1, the model term \(T - c \cdot df\) of every version being zero, and its tli, nnfi, and rmsea, which divide by the degrees of freedom and are 0/0, take lavaan's conventions for a model that fits exactly, 1 and 0, whatever the version, and no line under the table names a version for them, under FIML and after two-stage estimation as well (the srmr line and the two-stage lines on the test, the criteria, and the cases are kept). A model with no degrees of freedom whose statistic is not zero does not fit exactly, as when an inequality bound binds (lavaan's count of the degrees of freedom leaves it out): its cfi is formed from its statistic in the version its CFI alone decides, and its tli, nnfi, rmsea, and RMSEA limits, which divide by the degrees of freedom, are undefined and NA, as sem_fit_measures reports them, with a line under the table that says so. One factor of three variables correlated .8, .8, and .5, with bounds = "pos.var" passed through ..., has a statistic of 32.8 on 0 degrees of freedom (\(N\) = 200) and a cfi of .925; its tli, nnfi, rmsea, and RMSEA limits are NA, where lavaan reports the values of exact fit, 1 and 0, whenever the degrees of freedom are zero. Under FIML (missing = "ml" or "fiml") the chi_square row is the FIML likelihood ratio statistic (its scaled version with estimator = "MLR"), and those rows are lavaan's robust versions, which for a FIML fit are the corrected indices of Zhang and Savalei (2023): they evaluate the complete data fit function at the FIML estimates, with the saturated FIML estimates in place of the sample moments, and so approximate the indices complete data would give, where the usual indices computed from the chi_square row change with the amount of missing data. lavaan uses their version 6, which assumes normality, and their version 3, which does not, with estimator = "MLR". Zhang and Savalei define only the RMSEA and the CFI; the TLI, the NNFI, and the RMSEA interval are lavaan's extension of the same correction. lavaan cannot combine FIML with the Satorra-Bentler or the mean and variance adjusted statistic (test = "satorra.bentler" or "mean.var.adjusted" passed through ...); an explicit FIML request with one of them stops rather than returning a fit to the complete cases, and the default fits the items as they stand when none is missing (see missing). The srmr row is the SRMR of the covariance residuals alone (lavaan's srmr_bentler_nomean when the model has a mean structure), as sem_fit_measures reports it, so that the intercepts a FIML fit adds, whose residuals are zero, do not lower it (lavaan's srmr of a model with a mean structure averages the mean residuals in). With auxiliary variables (lavaan's aux under FIML) it is over the items alone, for the reason sem_fit_measures gives. A line under the printed table names the version of the indices after FIML with incomplete data, with estimator = "MLR", and after two-stage estimation, when they fall back from the robust ones, and when DMAR computed them.

Common row names under term: lambda_<factor>_<j> (loadings; lambda_<factor> when equated), psi_<factor>_<j> (error variances; psi_<factor> when equated), nu_<factor>_<j> (intercepts, when the mean structure is modeled; nu_<factor> when equated), phi_<factor> (factor variance, fixed to 1), phi_<factor1>_<factor2> (latent correlation), the per-factor defined parameters (loading_sum_<factor>, error_sum_<factor>, omega_<factor>, ave_<factor>, H_<factor>), and the fit rows chi_square, df, p_chi_square, cfi, tli, nnfi, rmsea, rmsea_ci_lower, rmsea_ci_upper, rmsea_ci_level, srmr, AIC, BIC, H0, H1.

Examples

data(holzinger_swineford)
hs_factors <- list(
  verbal    = c("t6_paragraph_comprehension", "t7_sentence",
                "t9_word_meaning"),
  deduction = c("t20_deduction", "t22_problem_reasoning",
                "t23_series_completion"))

# Congeneric measurement model for both factors (the default:
# nothing is constrained, and the header names the structure).
fa_confirmatory(holzinger_swineford, hs_factors)

# Equal loadings: equal_loading = TRUE equates the loadings within
# every factor, and a descriptor can also differ by factor, as here,
# where the verbal loadings are equated and the deduction loadings are
# left free. Because only the covariance structure identifies this
# constraint, the implied structure of the verbal factor is
# essentially tau-equivalent, and the header names each factor's
# structure separately.
fa_confirmatory(holzinger_swineford, hs_factors,
      equal_loading = c(verbal = TRUE, deduction = FALSE))

# Equal loadings and intercepts make the items tau-equivalent, and
# equal error variances as well make them parallel, the structure
# the header names here. The mean structure is added because
# equal_intercept asks about it, so the nu terms join the table.
fa_confirmatory(holzinger_swineford, hs_factors, equal_loading = TRUE,
      equal_intercept = TRUE, equal_error = TRUE)

# Ordered categorical items: two correlated factors of three
# four-category items each, generated here. The model is fit by WLSMV
# to polychoric correlations, and each ordered factor's omega is
# reported on the categorical sum score metric (categorical omega),
# which is why the interval columns of those two rows are NA.
set.seed(113)
n <- 200
eta_a <- rnorm(n)
eta_b <- 0.5 * eta_a + sqrt(1 - 0.5^2) * rnorm(n)
lambda <- c(0.6, 0.7, 0.8)
lat <- cbind(outer(eta_a, lambda), outer(eta_b, lambda)) +
  matrix(rnorm(n * 6), n, 6) %*% diag(sqrt(1 - c(lambda, lambda)^2))
likert <- as.data.frame(apply(lat, 2, function(x)
  as.integer(cut(x, breaks = c(-Inf, -1, 0, 1, Inf)))))
names(likert) <- paste0("item_", 1:6)
fa_confirmatory(likert,
      list(scale_a = paste0("item_", 1:3),
           scale_b = paste0("item_", 4:6)),
      ordered = TRUE, output = "measurement")
#> Ordered items declared: switching to estimator = "WLSMV" with robust standard errors.
#> omega_scale_a, omega_scale_b reported on the categorical sum score metric (categorical omega; Green & Yang, 2009; Kelley & Pornprasertmanit, 2016).
#> Measurement structure, per factor:
#>   scale_a: congeneric (no equality constraints)
#>   scale_b: congeneric (no equality constraints)
#> 
#>  syntax             term                 estimate se    test_statistic p_value 
#>  scale_a ~~ scale_b phi_scale_a_scale_b  0.427    0.084 5.089          < 0.0001
#>                     omega_scale_a        0.688    <NA>  <NA>           <NA>    
#>                     ave_scale_a          0.491    0.047 10.511         < 0.0001
#>                     H_scale_a            0.793    0.058 13.695         < 0.0001
#>                     omega_scale_b        0.762    <NA>  <NA>           <NA>    
#>                     ave_scale_b          0.576    0.040 14.362         < 0.0001
#>                     H_scale_b            0.843    0.045 18.788         < 0.0001
#>  scale_a ~~ scale_b htmt_scale_a_scale_b 0.412    <NA>  <NA>           <NA>    
#>  ci_lower ci_upper

#>  <NA>     <NA>    
#>  0.401    0.582   
#>  0.657    0.884   
#>  <NA>     <NA>    
#>  0.496    0.652   
#>  0.735    0.913   
#>  <NA>     <NA>    
#>

# Two-stage maximum likelihood with incomplete data, here 60 scores on
# one verbal test deleted at random. The chi_square row is the residual
# based statistic of Savalei and Bentler (2009), the cfi and rmsea rows
# are the normal theory analog of the two-stage indices of Zhang and
# Savalei (2023), and the lines under the table say which statistic,
# indices, and criteria are reported.
hs_incomplete <- holzinger_swineford
set.seed(113)
hs_incomplete$t7_sentence[sample(301, 60)] <- NA
fa_confirmatory(hs_incomplete, hs_factors, missing = "two_stage")

# Does the equal-loadings description hold? Two fits that differ only
# in a descriptor are nested, so output = "fit" hands them straight to
# lavaan's likelihood ratio test.
fit_free  <- fa_confirmatory(holzinger_swineford, hs_factors, output = "fit")
fit_equal <- fa_confirmatory(holzinger_swineford, hs_factors,
                   equal_loading = TRUE, output = "fit")
lavaan::lavTestLRT(fit_free, fit_equal)
